newsitem.title: USA: Administration proposes cutting subsidized rents.
newsitem.headline: Administration proposes cutting subsidized rents.

text.p: Saying it was inexcusable for the government to pay excessive rents for subsidised housing, officials proposed a bill Wednesday to roll back the rents while offering tax incentives to the landlords.
Andrew Cuomo, secretary of Housing and Urban Development, and Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin announced the measure they said could save taxpayers $1.4 billion over five years.

Cuomo said that under contracts negotiated in the 1970s, the federal government has been paying rent far above the market price for some 500,000 subsidised apartments for about 850,000 low-income people nationwide.

"To be subsidising rents which are higher than market rates is inexcusable," Cuomo said. But he said the government could not just reduce the rent because the landlords might default on their mortgages, which were insured by the government Federal Housing Administration.

"You (the taxpayer) would just be paying out of the other pocket" if such defaults occurred, Cuomo said. So Rubin's Treasury worked out a tax incentive plan to help lower rents while guarding against default.

Under the legislation, owners of subsidised housing who renegotiate their mortgages would be allowed to stretch out their tax bills that result from the mortgage restructuring over a period of up to 10 years.
In exchange, the owners would have to agree to keep 40 percent of their units affordable for families earning 60 percent of the median income, for a period of 15 years.
Rubin said the tax provisions would not add to the federal budget deficit.

The government has been paying far more than the market rental rates in many cities, Cuomo said. For example, in Washington, the government was paying $734 a month for apartments in federally-assisted housing with a market rental value of $499 to $549 a month.
The legislation would also allow HUD to crack down on poor housing conditions, and give the agency more flexibility to design innovative housing solutions, officials said.

Cuomo said his agency was seeking $5.6 billion this year for its entire portfolio of rent subsidy programmes, but he did not think this should be cut to pay for emergency funding for flood aid in the northern plains, where thousands of people have left their homes. Funding for both was needed, he said.

"We need to get people back in their houses in North Dakota. It does not mean that we should take people out of their homes in other parts of the country to create housing for people in North Dakota," Cuomo said.
